1.cue: purpose of the OSI physical layer
1.tip: Physical = bits on the wire. Frames and media access belong to the data link layer.
1.why: The physical layer turns bits into signals (electrical, light or radio) and sends them across the local media. Controlling access and checking frames happen one layer up, at data link.

2.tip: Two strands = two one-way streets: one to send, one to receive at the same time.
2.why: Light in a fiber travels one way only. With one strand for sending and one for receiving, both ends can talk at the same time, which is full-duplex.

3.tip: Crosstalk = wires talking across to their neighbors. Lighting is EMI, long cables is attenuation.
3.why: Crosstalk is when the signal in one wire leaks into the wire next to it and distorts it. Fluorescent lights cause EMI, and weakening over distance is attenuation.

4.tip: Twisted pair is named for its crosstalk cure: twist the pairs.
4.why: Twisting the two wires of a circuit together makes their magnetic fields cancel each other out, so they leak less into nearby pairs. This is called cancellation.

5.tip: Throughput drops with the 3 T's of the moment: how much Traffic, what Type, and Time delay (latency).
5.why: Bandwidth is the capacity. Throughput is what you really get, and it falls when lots of traffic is crossing, when the kind of traffic is demanding, and when many devices add delay.

6.tip: Fiber: immune to noise, heavy on the wallet.
6.why: Fiber carries light, not electricity, so electrical and radio interference can't affect it. It costs more than UTP. Foil and twisting are copper ideas.

7.cue: primary role of the Physical layer
7.tip: Physical layer = signal maker. Addressing and access control are data link, paths are network.
7.why: The physical layer takes the bits of each frame and turns them into signals on the media. Addressing, media access and path selection are done by higher layers.

8.tip: Current makes a magnetic field, and the field spills into the next pair.
8.why: Electricity flowing in a wire creates a magnetic field. That field can induce a signal in the neighbor pairs, which is crosstalk. Reflection and collisions are different problems.

9.cue: What type of cabling is shown
9.tip: Thin glass core with a strength jacket and no copper pairs: that's fiber.
9.why: The picture shows a cable with a glass core, cladding and protective layers, which is how fiber-optic cable is built. It has no twisted copper pairs.

10.cue: interfere with the communication carried over UTP
10.tip: Copper's two enemies: noise from inside (crosstalk) and noise from outside (EMI).
10.why: UTP carries electrical signals, so they can be distorted by nearby pairs (crosstalk) and by outside sources like motors and lights (EMI). Bandwidth and network size are not interference.

11.cue: What type of cabling is shown
11.tip: Colored twisted pairs, no foil or braid around them: Unshielded Twisted Pair.
11.why: The picture shows four pairs of colored wires twisted together with only a plastic jacket and no metal shielding, which is UTP.

12.tip: Wi-Fi's noisy neighbors use 2.4 GHz too: cordless phones and microwaves.
12.why: Microwave ovens and many cordless phones work in the same 2.4 GHz band as Wi-Fi, so they can interfere with wireless signals.

13.cue: services provided by the data link layer
13.tip: Data link: pack it (frame the packet) and place it (control access to the media).
13.why: The data link layer wraps Layer 3 packets in a frame that fits the interface, and it controls how frames get onto the media. End-to-end addressing is Layer 3, reliable delivery is Layer 4.

14.cue: CRC value that is found in the FCS
14.tip: CRC = Check Received Correctly: is the frame intact?
14.why: The sender calculates a CRC and puts it in the FCS. The receiver does the same math. If the numbers match, the frame arrived without damage.

15.tip: Header = addresses at the front. Trailer = error check at the back.
15.why: The frame trailer holds the FCS, which the receiver uses to detect errors. Addresses go in the header, and the data sits in the middle.

16.cue: frame header fields of the data link layer
16.tip: Ethernet, PPP and Wi-Fi frames all look different: headers vary by protocol.
16.why: Each data link protocol needs different control info, so the header fields change from one protocol to another. Ethernet headers hold MAC addresses, not Layer 3 addresses.

17.cue: connects some, but not all, remote sites
17.tip: Some, but not all = partial. Every site to every site = full mesh.
17.why: A partial mesh adds extra links between some sites for backup paths, giving high availability without the cost of connecting every site to every other site.

18.cue: passed to the data link layer or discarded by the NIC
18.tip: NIC tosses frames that are broken (bad FCS) or too small (under 64 bytes, a runt).
18.why: Ethernet drops a frame if its FCS shows an error or if it is smaller than the 64-byte minimum. Both mean the frame is damaged, often from a collision.

19.tip: Full-duplex = no taking turns, so no referee needed.
19.why: In full-duplex each side can send and receive at the same time on separate paths, so there are no collisions and no need to decide who talks. Half-duplex needs arbitration.

20.tip: Extended star = stars linked to stars: switches connect to other switches.
20.why: In an extended star, end devices connect to a central switch, and that switch connects to other central switches, so you get several stars joined together.

21.tip: LLC = Link to the Layer above: it tells which Layer 3 protocol is inside.
21.why: The LLC sublayer adds information that identifies the network layer protocol, so IPv4 and IPv6 can share the same NIC and media. Logical addressing is Layer 3.

22.cue: ways that media access control is used
22.tip: Ethernet = CD (detect), Wi-Fi 802.11 = CA (avoid). Contention is NOT deterministic.
22.why: Media access control puts frames on the media using rules set by data link protocols, and wired Ethernet uses CSMA/CD. Wi-Fi uses CSMA/CA, and controlled access has no collisions.

23.cue: encapsulation process, what occurs at the data link layer
23.tip: Layer 2 adds the MAC (physical) address. IP is Layer 3, port is Layer 4.
23.why: When the frame is built, the data link layer adds the source and destination MAC addresses, which are physical addresses. IP addresses and port numbers are added at higher layers.

24.tip: Ethernet frame = MAC, MAC, check. IP addresses live inside the packet, not the frame header.
24.why: An Ethernet header holds the destination and source MAC addresses, and the trailer holds the FCS for error checking. IP addresses belong to the Layer 3 packet.

25.tip: Carrier Sense Multiple ACCESS: the name says it.
25.why: CSMA/CD is a set of rules for when a device can put data on shared media, so it is an access method, not flow control or encoding.

26.tip: Every frame is a sandwich: header, data, trailer.
26.why: All data link frames have a header with control info, the data (the packet), and a trailer for error checking. Type field and CRC are details inside those parts.

27.cue: true about the CSMA/CD access method
27.tip: CSMA starts with Carrier Sense: listen first, then talk.
27.why: With CSMA/CD every device must check that the wire is quiet before sending. Collisions can still happen, all devices back off, and nobody gets priority after.

28.tip: MDIX = Media Dependent Interface CROSSover: it fixes the cable type for you.
28.why: Auto-MDIX lets a port detect the cable and swap its send and receive pairs, so either a straight-through or a crossover cable works. Speed and duplex use autonegotiation.

29.cue: leaves the web server if the final destination is PC1
29.tip: MAC addresses only go one hop: a frame to another network goes to your own gateway's MAC.
29.why: PC1 is on another network, so the server sends the frame to its default gateway. The destination MAC is the router's Fa0/0 on the server's side, 00-60-2F-3A-07-CC.

30.cue: 1000BASE-T port to a port connected to a 100Base-T
30.tip: Mixed speeds? Share the memory pool so fast ports can wait for slow ones.
30.why: Shared memory buffering puts all frames in one common buffer, so a frame from a fast port can wait there until a slower port is ready. It handles mixed speeds well.

31.cue: examples of the cut-through switching method
31.tip: Cut-through comes in two flavors: fast-forward (go now) and fragment-free (wait 64 bytes).
31.why: Both start forwarding before the whole frame arrives. Fast-forward sends after reading the destination MAC, and fragment-free waits for the first 64 bytes to skip collision fragments.

32.cue: receives the entire frame and performs a CRC check
32.tip: Store the whole frame, check it, then forward it.
32.why: Store-and-forward waits until the full frame is received, checks the CRC, and drops it if there is an error. Cut-through methods forward before the frame is complete.

33.tip: FCS = Frame Check Sequence: it checks for errors.
33.why: The FCS holds a CRC value. The receiver recalculates it, and if the values differ, it knows an error happened during sending or receiving and drops the frame.

34.tip: Fast-forward is the fastest: it reads just the destination MAC and goes.
34.why: Fast-forward switching starts sending as soon as it reads the destination MAC address, so it adds the least delay. Fragment-free waits for 64 bytes, store-and-forward waits for all.

35.cue: connecting two modern switches using a straight-through
keys: fastest speed that is supported by both
35.tip: New switches agree on the best common speed, go full-duplex, and auto-MDIX fixes the cable.
35.why: Modern switches autonegotiate to the fastest speed both support and to full-duplex. Auto-MDIX adjusts the port so the straight-through cable works without a crossover.

36.tip: Store-and-forward is slower but safer: it checks every frame for errors.
36.why: Because it receives the whole frame first, store-and-forward can check the CRC and drop bad frames. Cut-through is faster but forwards errors.

37.cue: part of the Ethernet frame is used to perform an error check
37.tip: Error check sits at the tail: CRC in the trailer.
37.why: The CRC value is in the FCS field of the frame trailer. The switch recalculates it and compares to find damaged frames. Header fields are for addressing and type.

38.cue: uses the CRC value in a frame
38.tip: Only the method that waits for the whole frame can see the CRC at the end: store-and-forward.
38.why: The CRC is at the very end of the frame. Only store-and-forward waits for the full frame, so it is the only method that checks the CRC.

39.cue: actions performed by a Cisco switch
39.tip: Switch rule: learn from the SOURCE, forward by the DESTINATION.
39.why: A switch learns which port a device is on by reading the source MAC of frames, then forwards frames using the destination MAC and its table. IP addresses are a router's job.

40.tip: LLC = software that talks Up. MAC = hardware that talks Down to the media.
40.why: LLC is handled in software (the NIC driver) and connects the data link layer to upper layer protocols. It's defined in IEEE 802.2, and frame placement is the MAC sublayer's job.

41.tip: MDIX = auto crossover: any cable type works.
41.why: Auto-MDIX detects the type of copper cable plugged in and adjusts the port, so you don't need a special crossover cable between like devices. Speed and duplex are separate features.

42.tip: Cut-through cuts the wait: lower latency for fast computing.
42.why: Cut-through starts forwarding before the whole frame arrives, so frames get through faster. That low delay suits high-performance computing. It does not drop bad frames.

43.tip: IPv4 multicast MACs start with 01-00-5E. All F's is broadcast.
43.why: Ethernet MAC addresses for IPv4 multicast always begin with 01-00-5E. FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF is broadcast, and the others are normal unicast addresses.

44.tip: Keep the twists right up to the connector: untwist as little as possible.
44.why: When the wire pairs are untwisted too far from the connector, they lose their crosstalk protection and the link gets noisy. Untwist only about 1.25 cm (half an inch).

45.tip: In the activity, check the MAC address table and match the MAC to its port: Fa0/11.
45.why: In the Packet Tracer activity, the switch's MAC address table (show mac address-table) lists which port each MAC was learned on. The host in question is found on Fa0/11.

46.tip: Attenuation = attention fades the farther you go: signal gets weaker with distance.
46.why: Attenuation means a signal loses strength as it travels farther along the media. Leakage between pairs is crosstalk, and travel time is latency.

47.cue: fiber preferable to copper cabling for interconnecting buildings
47.tip: Fiber between buildings: Far, Free of noise, Fat pipe. It's not cheap or easy to terminate.
47.why: Fiber carries light over long distances with high bandwidth and is not affected by electrical or radio noise. It costs more and is harder to terminate than copper.

48.why: Modulation changes a carrier wave using the signal wave so it can carry data, like how AM and FM radio work. IEEE and EIA/TIA are standards groups.

49.cue: capacity at which a medium can carry data
49.tip: Bandwidth = the size of the pipe (capacity). Throughput = what actually flows.
49.why: Bandwidth is the maximum amount of data a medium can carry per second. It describes capacity, not what you actually get.

50.cue: measure of the transfer of bits
50.tip: Throughput = what actually gets through over time.
50.why: Throughput is the real number of bits moved across the media in a set time. It is usually lower than bandwidth because of traffic and delay.

51.tip: Latency = late: the delay from point A to point B.
51.why: Latency is how long data takes to travel from one point to another, including all delays along the way. Bandwidth and throughput measure amounts, not time.

53.tip: Goodput = only the good (usable) data. Throughput minus overhead.
53.why: Goodput counts only the useful data that gets delivered, leaving out overhead like headers, setup and retransmissions. It is lower than throughput.

54.tip: Electricity runs on copper. Light runs on glass. Radio runs through air.
54.why: Copper cable carries data as electrical pulses on metal wires. Fiber uses light, and wireless uses the air.

55.tip: Light = fiber. Glass strands carry light pulses.
55.why: Fiber-optic cable sends data as pulses of light through thin strands of glass or plastic.

56.tip: Wireless signals need no cable: the medium is the air.
56.why: Microwave and other radio signals travel through the air, so air is the medium for wireless transmission.

57.cue: functions are performed at the MAC sublayer
57.tip: MAC = the hardware side: runs the NIC and adds the error-checking trailer. LLC = protocol ID and L2 control info.
57.why: The MAC sublayer works with the NIC hardware to send and receive on the media and adds the FCS trailer to detect errors. Identifying the Layer 3 protocol is LLC's job.

58.cue: MAC sublayer of the OSI data link layer? (Choose two.) [Case 2]
58.tip: MAC faces the media: it syncs nodes and works with many physical technologies. LLC faces up to the software.
58.why: The MAC sublayer deals with the physical side: it keeps sender and receiver in sync and adapts to different media types. Talking to upper layers and adding control info are LLC tasks.

59.cue: MAC sublayer of the OSI data link layer? (Choose two.) [Case 3]
59.tip: MAC = media side: sync the nodes and add the error trailer.
59.why: The MAC sublayer provides synchronization between nodes and adds the trailer with the FCS for error detection. Protocol identification and IPv4/IPv6 sharing are LLC functions.

60.cue: MAC sublayer of the OSI data link layer? (Choose two.) [Case 4]
60.tip: MAC faces down to the media: physical technologies and sync. LLC faces up to software.
60.why: The MAC sublayer handles the media: it fits many physical technologies and keeps the nodes synchronized. Adding control info and linking to upper software are LLC jobs.

61.cue: MAC sublayer of the OSI data link layer? (Choose two.) [Case 5]
61.tip: MAC = hardware side: the NIC and the physical technologies it connects to.
61.why: The MAC sublayer controls the NIC that sends and receives bits and works with different physical media. Protocol identification and L2 control info belong to LLC.

62.cue: functions are performed at the LLC sublayer
62.tip: LLC = Link to the Layer above: it labels the Layer 3 protocol so IPv4 and IPv6 share one NIC.
62.why: LLC marks which network layer protocol is in the frame, so IPv4 and IPv6 can use the same interface. Controlling the NIC and delimiting fields are MAC sublayer jobs.

63.cue: LLC sublayer of the OSI data link layer
63.tip: LLC adds control info and the protocol label. MAC does encapsulation, the NIC and physical tech.
63.why: LLC adds Layer 2 control information and identifies the network layer protocol in the frame. Data encapsulation, the NIC and physical technologies are MAC sublayer tasks.

64.cue: LLC sublayer of the OSI data link layer
64.tip: LLC = upper side: control info plus letting IPv4 and IPv6 share. Addressing, trailer and sync = MAC.
64.why: LLC adds control information and lets several Layer 3 protocols share one interface. MAC addressing, the error trailer and synchronization are MAC sublayer jobs.

65.cue: LLC sublayer of the OSI data link layer
65.tip: LLC = Link to the Layer above: IPv4/IPv6 sharing and L2 control info.
65.why: LLC sits between the network layer and the MAC sublayer. It adds control info and lets IPv4 and IPv6 share the same media. Physical tech, trailer and sync are MAC jobs.

keys: all ports except the ingress port
66.tip: All F's = broadcast = flood everywhere except where it came in.
66.why: FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF is the broadcast address, meant for every device. The switch floods it out all ports except the one it arrived on.

keys: all ports except the ingress port
67.tip: 01-00-5E = multicast. A basic switch floods multicast just like broadcast.
67.why: 01:00:5E starts a multicast MAC. Without extra features like IGMP snooping, a switch treats it like a broadcast and floods it out every port except the incoming one.

68.cue: host receives a frame with a destination MAC address of FF
68.tip: Broadcast is for everyone, so every host opens it.
68.why: A broadcast frame is addressed to all devices on the LAN, so each host that receives it accepts it and passes it up to be processed. Hosts don't forward frames.

69.cue: does have the source MAC address in the MAC table
69.tip: Already known source? Just reset its clock so it doesn't age out.
69.why: If the source MAC is already in the table on that port, the switch simply refreshes the entry's aging timer so it stays. It only adds new entries for unknown sources.

71.cue: destination MAC address it does not recognize
71.tip: Not my MAC, not my frame: drop it.
71.why: A host's NIC only accepts frames sent to its own MAC, broadcast or multicast groups it joined. Any other frame is simply discarded. Hosts don't forward or return frames.

72.cue: connect a PC to a switch port
72.tip: Unlike devices (PC to switch) = straight-through. Like devices = crossover.
72.why: A PC and a switch use different pins to send and receive, so a straight-through cable lines them up. Crossover is for like devices, and rollover is for the console.

73.cue: Match the situation with the appropriate use of network media
73.tip: Desks and horizontal runs = copper. Backbone and long-haul = fiber. Guests and waiting rooms = wireless.
73.why: Copper is cheap and fine for short runs to desks. Fiber handles high-speed backbones and long distances. Wireless suits places where people move around with their own devices.

74.cue: PC is connected to the console port of the switch
74.tip: Console = rollover. Switch to router = unlike = straight. Router to router = like = crossover.
74.why: A console connection uses a rollover cable. A switch and a router are unlike devices, so use straight-through. Two routers are like devices, so use crossover.
